post.title: Asking for Help Looks Braver Than You Think #shorts
post.description: Are you an 'I'm fine' person? Tell me in the comments. Send this to the friend who's 'fine' with everything. Omar almost didn't tell Grace 'I need help.' He was sure it would look weak. In 'Beautiful Mess Effect: Self–Other Differences in Evaluation of Showing Vulnerability' (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2018), Anna Bruk, Sabine Scholl and Herbert Bless asked people to imagine moments of vulnerability, like admitting a mistake, confessing feelings first or asking for help, either for themselves or for someone else. People judged their own vulnerability more negatively than the same move made by someone else, which they saw as more positive and more courageous. The researchers called it the beautiful mess effect. It doesn't mean every overshare goes well, but the risk you picture is often bigger than the one others see. #psychology #shorts #vulnerability #overthinking #mentalhealth

lines.text: Omar almost didn't tell Grace: 'I need HELP.'
You know the move: smile, say 'all good,' while you're SINKING.
But the thing you hide? Others see it as BRAVE.
In 2018, Anna Bruk's team had people imagine admitting a MISTAKE.

lines.text: Picturing themselves: WEAKNESS. Picturing others: courage.
It's called the beautiful MESS effect.
Think of a friend who admitted they were struggling. You didn't think 'weak.' You thought 'HUMAN.'
Omar says it. Grace just SMILES. Are you an 'I'm fine' person? Send this to the friend who's 'fine' with everything.
